Hi, everyone. I'm Xiaojing Wang from-
Can we all learn from me?
It's online
... Turin University Biodiversity Research Institute.
FishR is our repository for museum fish specimen
images, and the images produced from them through AI
processing. Most of that processing happens outside the
repository. When we bring the results into FishR, we need
to know which image was used as input and which
processing run created each result.
Today, I will show how we record and validate those two links in
our system.
Fishare is the image repository developed for the
biology guided neural networks and image omics
projects. Excluding test records, the current
database snapshot contains just over 400,000
source image records from 67 institutions
and seven source collections. It also contains about
306,000 derived images and roughly
290,000 bounding box images,
42,000 segmentations and 27,000 landmarks.
The source images are distributed across many collections,
but a number of project teams carried out the AI processing
pipelines, mostly outside Fishare.
The repository, therefore has to receive the output files together
with enough information to reconnect them to their
sources and processing history.
This figure follows one specimen through three AI processing tasks.
At the top is the digitized source image.
The first task produces a bounding box image.
That image is then used for segmentation, and the segmentation
result is used for landmark detection.
Each task produces a separate image record and
belongs to a separate processing batch.
Files can later be renamed or copied, so file names alone
cannot reliably preserve these relationships.
So in Fishare provenance for derived image records,
both its direct input image and its
processing run.
This diagram shows what moves between Fishare and the external
processing pipelines. The blue outline includes the image
sets stored in Fishare. At the top, images from
digitized collections enter the repository after cleaning and filtering.
The blue arrows show selected images moving from
Fishare to a processing pipeline.
The pink arrows show the resulting files returning to the
repository. When a team submits its results,
Fishare stores the output images together with one batch
record describing that run. Our current database contains
21 batch records for AI pipelines carried out from our
team and the Virginia Tech team.
Once the results are in Fishare, we use ArchIDs to preserve those
connections. An ArchID is an archival resource key, a
persistent identifier assigned to a record in Fishare.
ArchIDs connect each output to its
direct input image and to the batch record for that processing run.
For derived image records, we focus on its own ArchID and
two ArchID references stored with it.
They are parent ArchID and the
batch ArchID. The parent ArchID identifies the
image used directly in the current processing step.
Following this field from one record to the next reconstructs
the lineage back to the source image.
A source image has no parent ArchID, so that's where the chain
ends. The batch ArchID records how the image entered
Fishare. Derived images refer to the
processing batches, while harvested source images
refer to the harvest batches.
The parent chain reconstructs the sequence of the images, while
the batch records preserve the context of the event that added each
image to the repository.
This is one batch record from our system.
It describes a bounding box run completed at Virginia Tech on
February 3rd, 2022. Dr. Murrough is
listed as the creator, and BGN is
listed as the project. These fields shown here are
terms in the Fishare vocabulary: pipeline, institution,
creator, project, and the date. They describe the batch as a whole,
so the vocabulary defines batch as
its own class with 14 terms. Additional terms
include supplement paths for an extra metadata file
and code repository for the source code.
Software configuration and processing parameters can be included
in the supplementary file when it's available.
Also, this structure matters at scale.
The largest Fishare batch contains just under a quarter of a million
outputs. Fishare stores the shared metadata once
on the batch record, and each output
only needs the batch ArchID to refer back to it.
Again, this figure shows how ArchIDs connect images to their metadata.
On the left is the one parent and child chain from the source image
to landmarks. Each stage has its own ArchID.
The segmentation in the middle is shown again on the right.
Resolving its ArchID brings up the corresponding images,
records, and its metadata.
At the same time, those same connections remain in the downloadable
archive when a user download it,
such as in multimedia CSV. Every image
record includes its ArchID and
batch ArchID.
AI-derived images also include parent ArchID.
Batch CSV supplies the shared context for each batch.
The download also contains citation information, term
definition, and RDF model.
Fish Share Vocabulary Version 3 defines the provenance terms and
declares batch as a class. A user should not need
access to our internal database or a separate workflow
system to reconstruct these relationships.
The exported files carry the parent chain and the batch
references into another computing environment.
Those exported identifiers also make the relationships
easy to check automatically.
In our current database, we checked about
359,000 parent links and about
763,000 batch links. All of them
point to existing records, and no image has
itself as its parent. An early audit found 29
unresolved batch links, but all of them came from test
records, not the production dataset.
So we run the same checks after each batch is ingested
and before every export.
Also, once we know these links are complete, we can use them during
model analysis. If a result looks wrong, a
researcher can start with its ArchID and follow its lineage
back through the intermediate
images to the original specimen image.
The batch records show which pipeline run
produces each step. At the dataset level,
the same metadata lets researchers compare model performance
across source collections or across batches
within the same pipeline stage. They can
see whether a performance difference is
associated with the source material or with a particular
AI pipeline.
To summarize, Fish Share uses ArchID to keep two parts of
a provenance together, the image lineage and the pipeline
context. The parent chain records the lineage,
while the batch records provide the context.
Both remain in the exported data and Fish Share checks them
automatically. Researchers can therefore trace a result back to
its source specimen and understand the processing history
behind it.
